paragraphs: I.
‘But true or not, your brother is a scoundrel. No man—no decent man—tells things like that.’

‘He didn’t tell me. How dare you think that? I found the letter in his desk. Since she is my friend and you are her lover, I never imagined there could be any harm in reading her letter to my brother. Give me back the letter. I was a fool to tell you.’
Ida Helmont held out her hand for the letter.
‘Not yet,’ I said, and went to the window. The dull red of a London sunset burned on the paper as I read the distinctive, delicate handwriting I knew so well and had kissed so often—

‘Darling, I do—I do love you, but it’s impossible. I must marry Arthur. My honour binds me to him. If only he would set me free—but he never will. He loves me so foolishly. But it is you I love—body, soul and spirit. There is no one in my heart but you. I think of you all day and dream of you all night. And we must part. And that is the way of the world. Goodbye!—Yours, yours, yours,
ELVIRE.’
I had certainly seen that handwriting often enough. But the passion written there was new to me. That I had never seen.

I turned wearily from the window. My sitting room looked strange to me. There were my books, my reading lamp, my untouched dinner still on the table, just as I had left it when I rose to hide my surprise at Ida Helmont’s visit. Ida Helmont now sat in my armchair, watching me quietly.
‘Well—aren’t you going to thank me?’
‘You put a knife in my heart, and then ask for thanks?’
‘Forgive me,’ she said, lifting her chin. ‘I have done nothing but show you the truth. One should expect no gratitude for that. May I ask, out of mere curiosity, what you intend to do?’
‘Your brother will tell you—’
She suddenly stood, pale to the lips.
‘You won’t tell my brother?’ she began.
‘That you’ve read his private letters? Certainly not!’
She came towards me, her golden hair blazing in the sunset.
‘Why are you so angry with me?’ she said. ‘Be reasonable. What else could I do?’
‘I don’t know.’
‘Would it have been right not to tell you?’
‘I don’t know. I only know that you’ve put out the sun, and I haven’t got used to the dark yet.’
‘Believe me,’ she said, coming closer still and resting her hands on my shoulders with the lightest, lightest touch, ‘believe me, she never loved you.’
A softness in her voice irritated and stirred me. I moved gently back, and her hands fell to her sides.
‘I beg your pardon,’ I said. ‘I have behaved very badly. You were quite right to come, and I am not ungrateful. Will you post a letter for me?’
I sat down and wrote—
‘I give you back your freedom. It is the only gift of mine that can please you now.
‘ARTHUR.’
I held the sheet out to Miss Helmont. When she had glanced at it, I sealed, stamped and addressed it.

‘Goodbye,’ I said then, and gave her the letter. As the door closed behind her, I sank into my chair. I am not ashamed to say that I cried like a child or a fool over my lost plaything—the little dark-haired woman who loved someone else with ‘body, soul and spirit’.
I had heard neither the door opening nor a footstep, so I started when a voice behind me said—
‘Are you so terribly unhappy? Oh, Arthur, don’t think I’m not sorry for you!’
‘I don’t want anyone to be sorry for me, Miss Helmont,’ I said.
She was silent for a moment. Then, in a quick, sudden, gentle movement, she bent and kissed my forehead. I heard the door close softly. Then I knew that the beautiful Miss Helmont loved me.
At first, that thought only drifted past, a light cloud against a grey sky. But the next day, reason woke and said—
‘Was Miss Helmont telling the truth? Was it possible that—?’
I resolved to see Elvire, to learn from her own lips whether, by some happy chance, this blow had come not from her but from a woman whose love might have killed her honesty.

I walked from Hampstead to Gower Street. As I walked along that long street, I saw a figure in pink come out of one of the houses. It was Elvire. She walked ahead of me to the corner of Store Street, where she met Oscar Helmont. They turned and met me face to face, and I saw all I needed to see. They loved each other. Ida Helmont had told the truth. I bowed and walked on. Before six months had passed, they were married. Before a year was over, I had married Ida Helmont.

I do not know what brought it about. Perhaps it was remorse for having imagined, even for half a day, that she could be so base as to fabricate a lie to win a lover. Perhaps it was her beauty, or the sweet flattery of being chosen by a woman who had half her acquaintances at her feet. I do not know. Whatever the reason, my thoughts turned to her as to their natural home. My heart took the same road, and before long I loved her as I had never loved Elvire. Let no one doubt that I loved her—as, please God, I shall never love again!

There had never been anyone like her. She was brave and beautiful, witty and wise, and adorable beyond all measure. She was the only woman in the world. Her openness and generosity of heart made every other woman seem small and contemptible. She loved me, and I worshipped her. I married her, stayed with her for three golden weeks, and then left her. Why?

Because she told me the truth. It was late one night. We had spent the whole evening on the veranda of our seaside lodgings, watching the moonlight on the water and listening to the soft sound of the sea on the sand. I have never been so happy. I hope I shall never be happy again.
‘Heart of my heart,’ she said, resting her golden head against my shoulder, ‘how much do you love me?’
‘How much?’
‘Yes—how much? I want to know what place I hold in your heart. Am I more to you than anyone else?’
‘My love!’
‘More than yourself?’
‘More than my life!’
‘I believe you,’ she said. Then she drew a long breath and took my hands in hers. ‘It can make no difference. Nothing in heaven or earth can come between us now.’
‘Nothing,’ I said. ‘But, my sweet, my wife, what is it?’
For she was deathly pale.
‘I must tell you,’ she said. ‘I cannot hide anything from you now, because I am yours—body, soul and spirit.’
The phrase was an echo that stung me.
The moonlight shone on her golden hair, her warm, soft, golden hair, and on her pale face.
‘Arthur,’ she said, ‘do you remember me coming to you at Hampstead with that letter?’
‘Yes, my sweet, and I remember how you—’
‘Arthur!’ She spoke quickly and quietly. ‘Arthur, that letter was a forgery. She never wrote it. I—’

She stopped. I had stood up, flung her hands away and stood looking at her. God help me! I thought I felt anger at her lie. I know now that it was only wounded vanity that stung. That I should have been tricked, that I should have been deceived, that I should have been led into making a fool of myself! That I should have married the woman who had fooled me! At that moment, she was no longer the wife I adored. She was only a woman who had forged a letter and tricked me into marrying her.
I spoke; I condemned her; I said I would never speak to her again. I felt it rather did me credit to be so angry. I said I would have nothing more to do with a liar and a forger.

I do not know whether I expected her to crawl to my knees and beg for forgiveness. I think I had some vague idea that, in time, I could agree with dignity to forgive and forget. I did not mean what I said. No, no; I did not mean a word of it. While I was saying it, I longed for her to weep and fall at my feet, so that I could lift her and hold her in my arms again.
But she did not fall at my feet. She stood looking at me quietly.
‘Arthur,’ she said as I paused for breath, ‘let me explain—she—I—’

‘There is nothing to explain,’ I said angrily. I still had that foolish sense that there was something rather noble in my indignation, as one feels when calling oneself a miserable sinner. ‘You are a liar and a forger, and that is enough for me. I will never speak to you again. You have wrecked my life—’
‘Do you mean that?’ she interrupted, leaning forward to look at me. Tears lay on her cheeks, but she was not crying now.
I hesitated. I longed to take her in my arms and say, ‘Rest your head here, my darling. Cry here, and know how I love you.’
Instead, I said nothing.
‘Do you mean it?’ she insisted.
Then she put her hand on my arm. I longed to take it and draw her to me.
Instead, I shook it off and said—
‘Mean it? Yes—of course I mean it. Don’t touch me, please! You have ruined my life.’
Without a word, she turned away, went into our room and closed the door.
I longed to follow her and tell her that, if there was anything to forgive, I forgave it.
Instead, I went out onto the beach and walked away beneath the cliffs.

Before long, however, the moonlight and solitude brought me to a better frame of mind. Whatever she had done, she had done for love of me. I knew that. I would go home and tell her so. Whatever she had done, I would tell her, she was my dearest life, my heart’s one treasure. It was true that my ideal of her had been shattered. But even as she was, what was the whole world of women beside her? I hurried back. In my resentment and bad temper, though, I had walked far, and the way back was very long. By the time I opened the door of the little house where we lodged, we had been apart for three hours. The house was dark and very still. I slipped off my shoes, crept up the narrow stairs and opened our bedroom door very softly. Perhaps she would have cried herself to sleep. I would lean over her, wake her with kisses and beg her to forgive me. Yes, it had come to that now.

I entered the room; I went towards the bed. She was not there. One glance told me she was not in the room. Within two minutes, I knew she was not in the house. After wasting a priceless hour searching the town for her, I found a note on the dressing table—
‘Goodbye! Make the best of what is left of your life. I will spoil it no more.’

She was gone, utterly gone. I rushed to town on the earliest morning train, only to find that her family knew nothing of her. Advertisements failed. Only a tramp said he had met a white lady on the cliff, and a fisherman brought me a handkerchief marked with her name, which he had found on the beach.

I searched the country far and wide, but at last I had to return to London, and the months went by. I will not say much about those months. Even the memory of that suffering makes me faint and sick at heart. The police, detectives and newspapers failed me completely. Her friends could not help me. They were also furiously indignant with me, especially her brother, who was now living very happily with my first love.

I do not know how I survived those long weeks and months. I tried to write; I tried to read; I tried to live like a reasonable human being. But it was impossible. I could not bear other people’s company. Day and night, I almost saw her face, almost heard her voice. I took long walks in the country, and her figure was always just around the next bend in the road, in the next clearing in the wood. But I never quite saw her, never quite heard her. I believe I was not entirely sane then. At last, one morning, as I was setting out on another of those long walks whose only destination was exhaustion, I met a telegram delivery boy and took the red envelope from his hand.
On the pink paper inside was written—
‘Come to me at once. I am dying. You must come.—IDA.—Apinshaw Farm, Mellor, Derbyshire.’

There was a train at twelve to Marple, the nearest station. I took it. I tell you, some things cannot be written about. My life through those long months was one; that journey was another. What had her life been through those months? The question tormented me as the sight of a surgical operation or a wound inflicted on someone dear torments every nerve. But the overwhelming feeling was joy—intense, unspeakable joy. She was alive! I would see her again. I took out the telegram and looked at it: ‘I am dying.’ I simply did not believe it. She could not die before she had seen me. If she had lived all those months without me, she could live now, with me beside her again. She would know the hell I had endured away from her and the heaven of our reunion. She must live. I would not let her die.
There was a long drive over bleak hills. Dark, jolting, endlessly exhausting. At last, we stopped before a long, low building where one or two lights shone faintly. I jumped out.
The door opened. A blaze of light made me blink and draw back. A woman stood in the doorway.
‘Are you Arthur Marsh?’ she said.
‘Yes.’
‘Then you’re too late. She’s dead.’
II.

I went into the house, walked to the fire and held out my hands mechanically. Though it was a May night, I was cold to the bone. Some people stood around the fire, and lights flickered. Then an old woman came forward with the northern instinct for hospitality.
‘You’re tired,’ she said, ‘and dazed, by the look of you. Have a little tea.’

I burst out laughing. It was too funny. I had travelled two hundred miles to see her, and she was dead, and they offered me tea. They drew back as though I were a wild animal, but I could not stop laughing. Then a hand touched my shoulder. Someone led me into a dark room, lit a lamp, put me in a chair and sat opposite me. It was a bare sitting room, coldly furnished with rush-seated chairs and highly polished tables and cupboards. I caught my breath, suddenly grew serious and looked at the woman sitting opposite me.
‘I was Miss Ida’s nurse,’ she said. ‘She told me to send for you. Who are you?’
‘Her husband—’

The woman looked at me with hard eyes, in which intense surprise struggled with resentment. ‘Then may God forgive you!’ she said. ‘I don’t know what you’ve done, but forgiving you will be hard work—even for Him!’
‘Tell me,’ I said, ‘my wife—’

‘Tell you?’ The bitter contempt in her voice did not hurt me. What was it beside the self-contempt that had gnawed at my heart all these months? ‘Tell you? Yes, I’ll tell you. Your wife was so ashamed of you that she never even told me she was married. Rather than that, she let me think whatever I liked. She just came here and said, “Nurse, look after me, for I am in terrible trouble.” “And don’t let them know where I am,” she said. Since I’m well married to an honest man and comfortably off here, I was able to do it, thanks to God’s blessing.’
‘Why didn’t you send for me before?’ The anguished cry was torn from me.

‘I would never have sent for you. That was her doing. Oh, to think that God Almighty has made men able to measure out such quantities of trouble for us women! Young man, I don’t know what you did to make her leave you, but it must have been cruel, for she loved the ground you walked on. Day after day, she used to sit looking at your picture, talking to it and kissing it when she thought I wasn’t watching, and crying until she made me cry too. She used to cry almost all night. And one day, when I told her to pray to God to help her through her troubles, she brought out your pretty face on a card, she did, and said, with her poor little smile, “That’s my god, Nursey,” she said.’
‘Don’t!’ I said weakly, holding out my hands to ward off the torture. ‘No more, not now.’

‘Don’t?’ she repeated. She had stood up and was walking up and down with her hands clasped. ‘Don’t, indeed! No, I won’t, but I shan’t forget you! I tell you, I’ve had you in my prayers time and again, when I thought you had made my darling your mistress. I shan’t leave you out now that I know she was your own wedded wife, whom you threw away when you tired of her and left to eat her heart out with longing for you. Oh, I pray to God above us to make you pay in full for everything you did to her! You killed my pretty girl. You will have to pay the price, young man, down to the very last farthing! O God in heaven, make him suffer! Make him feel it!’
She stamped her foot as she passed me. I stood perfectly still. I bit my lip until I tasted blood, hot and salty on my tongue.

‘She was nothing to you!’ cried the woman, walking faster up and down between the rush-seated chairs and the table. ‘Any fool can see that with half an eye. You didn’t love her, so you don’t feel anything now. But someday you’ll care for someone, and then you’ll know what she felt—if there’s any justice in heaven!’
I too stood, crossed the room and leaned against the wall. I heard her words without understanding them.

‘Can’t you feel anything? Are you made of stone? Come and look at her lying there so quietly. She doesn’t pine for the likes of you any more now. She won’t sit looking out of the window any more, saying nothing, only dropping her tears one by one, slowly, slowly into her lap. Come and see her. Come and see what you’ve done to my pretty girl—and then you can go. Nobody wants you here. She doesn’t want you now. But perhaps you’d like to see her safely underground first? I’m sure you’ll put a big slab over her—to make certain she doesn’t rise again.’
I turned on her. Her thin face was white with grief and helpless rage. Her claw-like hands were clenched.
‘Woman,’ I said, ‘have mercy!’
She paused and looked at me.
‘What?’ she said.
‘Have mercy!’ I said again.

‘Mercy? You should have thought of that before. You had no mercy on her. She loved you—she died loving you. If I weren’t a Christian woman, I’d kill you for it, like the rat you are! I would, even if I had to hang for it afterwards.’
I caught her hands and held them tightly, despite her resistance.

‘Don’t you understand?’ I said savagely. ‘We loved each other. She died loving me. I have to live loving her. And it’s her you pity. I tell you, it was all a mistake—a stupid, stupid mistake. Take me to her, and for pity’s sake leave me alone with her.’
She hesitated, then spoke in a voice only slightly less hard—
‘Well, come along, then.’
We moved towards the door. As she opened it, I heard a faint, weak cry. My heart stood still.
‘What’s that?’ I asked, stopping on the threshold.
‘Your child,’ she said curtly.
That too! Oh, my love! Oh, my poor love! All these long months!

‘She always said she would send for you when she was through her trouble,’ the woman said as we climbed the stairs. ‘“I’d like him to see his little baby, nurse,” she said. “Our little baby. It’ll be all right when the baby’s born,” she said. “I know he’ll come to me then. You’ll see.” And I never said anything. I didn’t think you would come if she was someone you’d used and left, and never dreamt you could be her husband and stay away from her for an hour, with her as she was. Hush!’

She took a key from her pocket and fitted it into the lock. She opened the door, and I followed her in. It was a large, dark room full of old-fashioned furniture. Wax candles stood in brass candlesticks, and there was a smell of lavender.
The big four-poster bed was covered in white.
‘My lamb—my poor pretty lamb!’ said the woman, starting to cry for the first time as she drew back the sheet. ‘Doesn’t she look beautiful?’

I stood beside the bed and looked down at my wife’s face. Just like that, I had seen it lying on the pillow beside me in the early morning, when the wind and dawn came up from beyond the sea. She did not look dead. Her lips were still red, and I thought there was a trace of colour in her cheek. It also seemed that, if I kissed her, she would wake, put her slender hand on my neck and rest her cheek against mine. We would tell each other everything, weep together, understand and find comfort.
So I bent and pressed my lips to hers as the old nurse slipped from the room.
But the red lips were like marble, and she did not wake. She will never wake again now.
I tell you again: some things cannot be written.
III.

That night I lay in a large room filled with heavy, dark furniture, in a great four-poster hung with heavy, dark curtains. The bed was the counterpart of that other bed, from whose side they had finally dragged me.
I believe they fed me, and the old nurse was kind to me. I think she now saw that it is not the dead who deserve the greatest pity.

At last I lay in the big, spacious bed and heard the household noises grow fewer and die away. My child’s little wail was the last. They had brought the child to me. I had held it in my arms and bowed my head over its tiny face and delicate fingers. I did not love it then. I told myself it had cost me her life. But my heart told me I had done that. The tall clock at the head of the stairs struck the hours—eleven, twelve, one—and still I could not sleep. The room was dark and very still.
I had not been able to look calmly at my life. Grief had intoxicated me—a real drunkenness, more merciful than the calm that follows.

Now I lay as still as the dead woman in the next room, looking at what remained of my life. I lay still and thought, and thought, and thought. In those hours, I tasted the bitterness of death. It must have been about two when I first became aware of a faint sound that was not the ticking clock. I say I first became aware of it, yet I knew perfectly well that I had heard it more than once before. I had determined not to hear it because it came from the next room—the room where the corpse lay.

I did not want to hear that sound because I knew it meant I was nervous—miserably nervous—a coward and a brute. I had killed my wife as surely as if I had put a knife into her breast. Now I had sunk so low as to fear her dead body—the dead body lying in the room next to mine. The heads of the beds stood against the same wall. From that wall, I had imagined hearing faint, faint, almost inaudible sounds. So when I say I became aware of them, I mean that I finally heard a sound too distinct for any doubt or question. It brought me upright in bed. Heavy drops of sweat gathered on my forehead and fell onto my cold hands as I held my breath and listened.
I do not know how long I sat there. There was no further sound. At last, my tense muscles relaxed and I fell back on the pillow.

‘You fool!’ I told myself. ‘Dead or alive, isn’t she your darling, the heart of your heart? Wouldn’t you nearly die of joy if she came to you? Pray to God to let her spirit return and tell you she forgives you!’
‘I wish she would come,’ I answered myself aloud, while every fibre of my body and mind shrank and trembled in denial.

I struck a match, lit a candle and breathed more freely as I looked at the polished furniture, the everyday details of an ordinary room. Then I thought of her lying alone, so close to me, so still beneath the white sheet. She was dead; she would not wake or move. But suppose she did move? Suppose she pulled back the sheet, got up, walked across the floor and turned the door handle?

As I thought it, I heard—clearly, unmistakably heard—the door of the room of death slowly open. I heard slow footsteps in the passage, slow, heavy footsteps. I heard hands touching the outside of my door, uncertain hands feeling for the latch.
Sick with terror, I lay gripping the sheet in my hands.

I knew well enough what would enter when that door opened, that door on which my eyes were fixed. I dreaded looking, yet dared not turn my eyes away. The door opened slowly, slowly, slowly, and the figure of my dead wife came in. It came straight towards the bed and stood at its foot in white burial clothes, with a white bandage beneath its chin. There was a scent of lavender. Its eyes were wide open, looking at me with unspeakable love.
I could have screamed aloud.
My wife spoke. It was the same dear voice I had loved so much to hear, but now it was very weak and faint. Now I trembled as I listened.

‘You aren’t afraid of me, darling, are you, even though I’m dead? I heard everything you said when you came, but I couldn’t answer. Now I’ve come back from the dead to tell you. I wasn’t really as bad as you thought. Elvire had told me she loved Oscar. I only wrote the letter to make things easier for you. I was too proud to tell you when you were so angry, but I’m not proud any more now. You’ll love me again now, won’t you, now that I’m dead? People always forgive the dead.’
The poor ghost’s voice was hollow and faint. Utter terror paralysed me. I could not answer.
‘Say you forgive me,’ the thin, monotonous voice went on. ‘Say you love me again.’
I had to speak. Coward though I was, I managed to stammer—
‘Yes, I love you. I have always loved you, God help me!’
The sound of my own voice reassured me, and I finished more firmly than I had begun. The figure beside the bed swayed a little unsteadily.
‘I suppose,’ she said wearily, ‘you would be afraid, now that I’m dead, if I came round to you and kissed you?’
She moved as though she were going to come to me.
Then I did scream aloud, again and again. I covered my face with the sheet, wound it around my head and body and held it with all my strength.

There was a moment’s silence. Then I heard my door close, then footsteps and voices, and I heard something heavy fall. I freed my head from the sheet. My room was empty. Then reason returned to me. I leapt out of bed.
‘Ida, my darling, come back! I’m not afraid! I love you! Come back! Come back!’

I sprang to the door and flung it open. Someone was bringing a light along the passage. On the floor outside the door of the room of death lay a huddled heap—the corpse in its burial clothes. Dead, dead, dead.
She is buried in Mellor churchyard, with no stone over her.

Whether it was catalepsy, as the doctors said, or whether my love returned even from the dead to me, who loved her, I shall never know. But this I do know: if I had held out my arms as she stood at the foot of my bed; if I had said, ‘Yes, even from the grave, my darling—from hell itself, come back, come back to me!’; if my coward’s heart had held room for anything but the unreasoning terror that killed love in that hour, I would not be here alone now. I shrank from her; I feared her; I would not take her to my heart. And now she will not come to me again.
Why do I go on living?
You see, there is the child. It is four years old now, and it has never spoken and never smiled.
